newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac to the rescue, but has he an alternative?
newsitem.headline: Chirac to the rescue, but has he an alternative?

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac is riding to the rescue of his centre-right coalition's flagging election campaign, but political analysts wonder whether the Gaullist leader has an alternative strategy.

Two weeks after Chirac plunged France into a surprise campaign, 10 months ahead of schedule, his gamble on winning a reduced but solid parliamentary majority for the rest of his seven-year term looks increasingly risky.

To avert the prospect of power-sharing with a hostile left-wing government, Chirac has chosen to intervene personally, with a policy article in provincial newspapers, to put his drive for a rejuvenated conservative majority back on the rails.
Aides say he is leaving open the possiblity of a public speech or televised appeal to voters after he returns from a visit to China on May 18 and before the first round of voting on May 25.

Opinion polls show the opposition Socialists and Communists neck-and-neck with the RPR-UDF coalition and gaining slowly amid widespread voter gloom or indifference, with the risk of a low turnout, particularly among young people.
A SOFRES institute poll showed that 64 percent of voters consider Chirac's record in the two years since his election to be negative, although many find him personally likeable.
Voters are not convinced by his explanation that an early election, contrary to French tradition, was needed to prepare for forthcoming decisions on European integration and economic reforms.
Why, they ask, will it be easier to pursue the same policies with a smaller majority than it was with the huge four-fifths majority which the conservatives have held since 1993?

This makes them receptive to opposition charges that the government is secretly planning a new wave of austerity as soon as the election is over to prepare France for a single European currency in 1999.
It may also fuel protest votes for the extreme-right National Front and for anti-Maastricht candidates fielded by maverick rightist Philippe de Villiers.
Chirac's prime minister and closest associate, Alain Juppe, has turned out to be a liability in opinion polls and a plum target for the left-wing opposition.
Socialist warnings against "five more years of Juppe" have prompted coalition strategists to hint Chirac might turn to a different premier.
But can he? And if he can't, what other means does he have to influence the outcome?
Most political commentators say that to abandon Juppe now, or even hint at dropping him would undermine voters' confidence in the coalition further.
It is also not in Chirac's nature. He has stood by his prime minister loyally and the two men's senior aides are piloting the campaign together from the Elysee presidential palace.
Nor is he likely to change policy, since he has staked his future on leading France into a single European currency and preserving its welfare system while easing in market reforms.
There is also a dearth of credible alternative premiers.
Gaullist Justice Minister Jacques Toubon, 55, is close to Chirac, but his image has been dented by having to ward off corruption investigations lapping at the coalition's ankles.
An opinion poll on Tuesday suggested Toubon could even lose his parliamentary seat in Paris, where he is running level with a previously unknown Socialist challenger.
Gaullist heavyweight Philippe Seguin, 54, spooks financial markets with his interventionist, anti-Maastricht rhetoric.
Juppe's predecessor as prime minister, Edouard Balladur, remains popular among voters. But Chirac is unlikely to appoint Balladur, his main Gaullist rival in a bitter 1995 presidential race.

Free-marketeering former finance minister Alain Madelin, 51, the darling of the business community, is regarded as too radical and too hostile to the welfare state to be electorally safe in a country attached to its strong state.

Centrist Force Democrate party leader Francois Bayrou, 46, is a good explainer and has been the first education minister in years to achieve reform without triggering student protests or teachers' strikes. But he is seen as a potential presidential rival by Chirac's Gaullist supporters.
The same applies to former defence minister Francois Leotard, 55, the leader of the centre-right Union for French Democracy which is junior partner in the coalition.
Without an alternative policy or an alternative prime minister, Chirac may have to dramatise the risk of political paralysis if a left-wing government is elected.
But since France has survived two periods of left-right "cohabitation" under the late president Francois Mitterrand, the prospect no longer scares the electorate, polls show.
